bull_bear.body: Growth is self-funded by design: negative working capital, ~six days debtors, float income from tenant security deposits, and net debt of just INR 5.6 cr. India cash flows are deployed into the domestic platform; international growth funds itself from international cash flows — the Work Studio acquisition was paid for entirely out of Singapore-generated cash. The INR 33 cr of security deposits paid to landlords this quarter is capital allocated to securing FY28 and FY29 supply — "We are paying today to own tomorrow's growth."
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Seat retention of 74% is the number that will be picked at.** Management's defence is that churn is deliberate portfolio rebalancing and mark-to-market repricing, that occupied seats rose, and that committed occupancy of mature centres remains 92% because replacement tenants are already found. Last year's full-year retention was 80–88% after a similarly weak first half.
- Occupancy dipped to 81% from 82% and is guided to 80–85% for three quarters — new-building fill, but it caps the reported metric during the heaviest growth phase.
- FCF is negative INR 56 cr and OCF/EBITDA fell below 1x. Both are explained by growth investment, but they are the first negative prints since listing.
- Concentration in H2: the guidance depends on Eastbridge and Eastside landing on schedule and pre-fills converting.
- Client-mix transition is deliberate but ongoing — IT/ITES fell from 44% to 35% over three years, and management could not break out call-centre exposure within IT/ITES when asked about AI-driven renewal risk.
- The margin-not-dilutive-at-scale claim has only been tested through one heavy capex quarter.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Confident and unusually well-instrumented — the team quoted third-party market data (Cushman & Wakefield flex-share series), gave a specific realisation number (INR 181/sq ft vs INR 170 prior year) unprompted, and directed analysts to specific presentation slides repeatedly. Notably, the transcript carries **nine numbered footnote corrections** where management corrected its own misstatements on the call (occupancy figures, seat counts, retention wording, an incorrectly named asset) — a level of transcript hygiene that is itself a governance signal. Neetish Sarda answered the conservatism challenge on guidance head-on rather than accepting the flattery. Harsh Binani was explicit that VAS upside is *not* in the numbers, which is the right way to handle an unproven line.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- The retention/occupancy pair must be read together: a 74% retention number alongside 92% committed occupancy and rising occupied seats means the company is actively repricing legacy tenants out, not losing them involuntarily. The metric will look bad in H1 and recover by year-end, as it did last year.
- VAS is structurally more attractive than it looks because it is take-rate, not resale — no cost sits on the books, so it hits the bottom line directly. It tripled YoY and is explicitly excluded from guidance.
- The GCC revenue already booked understates the opportunity: the services layer for signed GCCs has not started billing because most offices are still under fit-out — "the value accretion of the other services over and above the space will happen… over the next two or three quarters."
- Management is holding back a 10–15% pricing lever versus the nearest competitor, choosing volume and campus fill over rate.
- Landlord mix is ~65% non-institutional / 35% institutional and is expected to stay roughly there — the institutional share is the completion hedge, not the whole strategy.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- "Expansion Is Self-Funded" — gross debt INR 2,134 Mn and net debt of just INR 56 Mn ("Virtually debt-free"), against normalised equity of INR 9,747 Mn and normalised capital employed of INR 9,803 Mn.
- Cost of borrowing <9%, with CARE Rating A, "Upgraded earlier in year".
- Negative working-capital model with ~6-day debtors; normalised OCF/normalised EBITDA "Structurally above 1x", with quarterly dips attributed to security deposits paid to landlords for upcoming campuses through FY27-FY29 — "a choice, not a leak".
- Gross block bridge as on 30 Jun 2026: reported gross block INR 23,062 Mn less fitout cost capitalised INR (6,328) Mn plus other Ind-AS adjustments INR 56 Mn = normalised gross block INR 16,791 Mn (+29% YoY); normalised accumulated depreciation INR (5,489) Mn; normalised net block INR 11,302 Mn.
- Returns framed on three lenses across FY24 → Q1 FY27: RoCE 1.6% → 7.3% → 16.0% → 21.5%; Operating RoIC 1.4% → 6.6% → 16.4% → 22.9%; Cash RoCE 31.3% → 34.6% → 40.5% → 38.8%.

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Asset-liability mismatch between long-tenure landlord leases and shorter client contracts — Management names this the principal structural risk in the industry: the Company commits to entire buildings on 10-15 year master leases while client lock-ins run around 36 months, so a gap between locked-in client revenue receivable and locked-in landlord rental payable would expose the platform. It is monitored through locked-in rental coverage ratios, and the newer still-ramping footprint sits at only ~1.0 times cover versus more than 2.6 times on the mature footprint.
- Occupancy ramp-up risk on the new, immature footprint — Profitability is directly driven by centre maturity, and new centres carry a ramp-up drag until they cross breakeven and payback at 30-32 months. The new footprint stood at 1.2 Msf on 56% committed occupancy against 93% on the mature footprint, so any slippage in filling new centres delays margin and return conversion.
- Client concentration risk — The model depends on a limited number of large enterprise occupiers, where a single move-out can leave material vacancy. The Company mitigates this structurally - Top 10 client revenue reduced from ~39% in FY 2018-19 to ~20% in FY 2025-26, and no single client typically occupies more than 30% of any large centre (>0.20 Msf) - but the exposure remains inherent to a large-format campus model.
- Cyclicality of commercial real estate occupancy and rental rates — Management explicitly flags cyclical fluctuations in occupancy and rental rates as characteristic of commercial real estate markets. Long-term contractual agreements with both landlords and clients are the stated buffer, but a downturn would still pressure renewals, pricing and the pace of new leasing.
- Dependence on access to high-quality Grade A buildings in prime micro-markets — The Managing Director states that access to high-quality buildings will remain the industry's defining constraint, with demand exceeding new completions across key markets. Growth is contingent on continuing to secure suitable bare-shell buildings ahead of competitors; uninterrupted access to secured supply is described as the operational moat, and losing it would directly cap expansion.
- Sector concentration in IT/ITeS and single-activity business concentration — IT and technology services still represent ~39% of rental revenue (down from ~44% in FY 2023-24), and 100% of turnover comes from a single business activity - other business support services - so the Company has no diversification outside managed workspace to absorb a sector-specific shock.
- Intensifying competition and segment consolidation — The MD&A states competition is expected to intensify as the segment scales, with the top ten operators' share of flex leasing rising from 67% in 2024 to approximately 74% by H1 2026. Scale, balance-sheet strength and developer relationships have become the price of entry, raising the cost of staying competitive.
- High employee attrition and dependence on execution talent — The permanent employee turnover rate stood at 42% in the current financial year (46% in the prior year), and worker-level operational requirements are managed entirely through 3,404 contract workers. Consistent service standards across an expanding centre network depend on retaining and rebuilding this capability.
- AI-driven uncertainty in corporate headcount and workspace planning — Management notes AI is changing workforce composition at a pace that makes long-term headcount forecasting more difficult, and that the principal real-estate implication is greater uncertainty rather than a deterministic increase in office demand - compressing occupier planning horizons to three years or less for roughly 75% of large MNCs.
- Data privacy, cyber-security and regulatory compliance exposure — The Company operates technology-enabled workspaces holding sensitive data of employees, clients and partners, and states it is currently working on compliance with the DPDP rules. An Information Security Policy covering access controls, encryption, network protection and vulnerability assessment is the stated mitigation.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body:
- **India core rental (~92% of rental revenue is enterprise annuity demand):** 1,000+ seat cohort on 48-month tenures expanding across cities. Client mix deliberately diversified away from IT/ITES toward manufacturing, engineering, business consultancy and professional services; the stated target range for IT/ITES is 25–35%.
- **GCC:** 21% of revenue from 15% in FY26, described as the primary growth driver for the next two to three years. Clients now include a large Swiss bank, a manufacturing GCC and, this quarter, the subsidiary of a leading Japanese NBFC at the Mumbai campus. Demand is broadening beyond the US into Europe and Japan.
- **Value-added services / SmartVantage:** non-lease rental revenue tripled to INR 68 cr from INR 22 cr. Two large SmartVantage contracts won. Critically, the model is **take-rate based** — third parties provide the service, Smartworks takes a cut with no expense on its books, so it flows straight to the bottom line.
- **Singapore:** Work Studio acquired at cost of construction (it was at ~60% occupancy); Singapore now ~1,500 seats, ~80,000 sq ft, ~2% of revenue, with 400–450 seats available to sell. Explicitly not a scale market — "Not meaningfully… it's not going to go from 80,000 to 160,000 or 200,000." Funded entirely from Singapore cash flows with no risk on the Indian balance sheet.

business.body:

At 10.4 mn sq ft operational the company claims the largest platform in the industry, earning preferred landlord terms and lower unit costs.
- **Getting the right building first:** "For the past 4 to 5 years, demand for office space in our micro-markets has outpaced the availability of new office buildings. In a market running short of quality office supply, getting the right building first is the biggest advantage."

business.body:

business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Risk mitigation] Asset-liability mismatch: committed client lock-in revenue covers landlord lock-in rentals ~2.7x on the mature footprint, ~0.8x on the new footprint and ~2x overall — "No funding gap through FY29". Mature footprint 9.1 Msf at 92% committed occupancy carries committed revenue from clients of INR 47,077 Mn; operational footprint 10.4 Msf at 86% carries INR 53,909 Mn.
- [Risk mitigation] Built-in safeguards: typically no more than ~30% of a centre leased to a single client (cap applies to centres over 0.20 Msf); pricing targets rental revenue of at least 2x rental expense; long-term agreements with both landlords and clients; value pricing to stay preferred partner in downturns.
- [Technology] Proprietary stack runs the full lifecycle — Nexus (AI-led property/market discovery and pricing; 200+ properties evaluated, 4.7 Msf booked), WorkBlock (AI-powered design and standardised digital build; 3.5 Msf+ delivered in a year, 45-60 day go-live) and WorkCtrl (digital operating system for smart building operations, building intelligence and automation, workspace experience and digital service management).
- [Market — third party] Deck cites India office stock ~1,055 Msf growing +6.2% YoY versus India flex stock ~110-114 Msf growing +23-25% YoY (flex stock as of Dec'25) and Smartworks at +44% YoY on 14.5 Msf leased; flex was the #1 occupier at 27% of Q2 2026 leasing, ahead of Technology at 21%. Sources cited: CBRE, Knight Frank, Colliers, Redseer, EY, Nasscom, Bloomberg.

latest_quarter.body: Margin expanded to 19.6% from 16.2% a year ago on three drivers: centre maturity, cost-excellence initiatives particularly in energy (solar adoption across campuses), and operating leverage at both centre and corporate level. outlook.body:

Management defended the apparent conservatism directly — with committed occupancy at 92% there is little to sell on the existing base, so growth depends on new centres that take ~12 months to ramp: "you will see maybe Q3 or mostly Q4 see that jump."
- **Margin:** normalized EBITDA margin **19% to 20%** for the full year.
- **Footprint:** operational footprint of **over 13 mn sq ft by March 2027**, i.e. 2.5–3.0 mn sq ft added in FY27. Already 3.5 mn sq ft signed and under or entering construction — a buffer of 700,000–800,000 sq ft against project delays. 1.9 mn sq ft currently under fit-out.
- **Capex:** **INR 550–600 cr for FY27**, covering both fresh fit-outs and the three-yearly refurbishment cycle. New fit-out capex INR 1,350/sq ft, rising ~5% a year on inflation; refurbishment ~15% of initial capex every three years.
- **Occupancy:** "anywhere between 80% to 85% is where we can effectively look at our occupancies throughout the next three quarters, despite the high growth."
- **ROCE:** expected to expand meaningfully through FY28 as the current capex cohort matures and completes payback.
- **SmartVantage / VAS:** services revenue expected to "meaningfully double over the next two years" — but explicitly **not** factored into current-year projections.
- **Commissioning:** ~3 mn sq ft comes online over the next nine months, including Eastbridge (Vikhroli, Mumbai — 8.15 lakh sq ft, claimed as the world's largest standalone managed campus) and Eastside (Pune), both landing in H2 FY27 with strong pre-fills.

outlook.body: Two demand engines were laid out and both are already in the client base rather than prospective. First, flex is consolidating: India recorded its highest ever quarterly leasing at 24.6 mn sq ft with 27% through flex (up from 19% a year ago), and within flex the top-10 operators' share climbed from 67% in 2024 to 72% in 2025 and 74% in H1 of this year, with the long tail below 5% and shrinking. Second, AI and GCCs are expanding office demand outright — the AI workforce inside India's GCCs is set to grow fourfold by 2030, and that demand lands in exactly the collaboration-rich campuses Smartworks builds. Management's summary arithmetic: commercial real estate growing >6%, flex growing 23%, Smartworks growing 44% — "roughly seven times the office market and twice the Flex market."
outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Grow only where demand is already visible - expansion is executed against revenue and buildings already signed rather than against forecast demand, so tomorrow's campuses are contracted today
- Concentrate on large-format, campus-scale managed offices for mid-to-large enterprises rather than small-seat coworking, deliberately moving away from traditional volatile coworking layouts
- Lease entire buildings on tenures of up to 15 years to secure preferred landlord terms, walk-to-work positioning in prime clusters and a lean centralised cost structure with one operations team, one technology layer and one set of amenities
- Deepen three highest-quality demand cohorts - Global Capability Centres, the 1,000+ seat large-format cohort, and multi-city relationship clients - because each strengthens tenure, deal size and stickiness simultaneously
- Deliberately reduce IT/ITeS exposure and diversify into business consulting, engineering and manufacturing, and BFSI
- Scale capital-light monetisation beyond the seat: SmartVantage GCC enablement, and Value-Added Services and Fit-out-as-a-Service delivered largely on a take-rate basis through partners
- Let margin expansion come from portfolio maturity rather than pricing action, holding corporate and platform costs broadly flat over a materially larger base
- Build a common digital operating layer across real estate, design, projects, buildings, customers and operations - Nexus RE for growth decisions, WorkBlock for delivery, WorkCtrl for operations - increasingly augmented by AI
- Maintain financial discipline: fund growth internally where possible, keep leverage conservative, and pursue growth responsibly off a net-cash balance sheet
- Be selective rather than ubiquitous - not present everywhere, but the obvious choice for large clients in the markets that matter
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Smartworks expanded its total super built-up area from 11.8 Msf at March 2025 to 16.1 Msf at March 2026 across 66 centres in 15 cities including Singapore, adding roughly 4.3 Msf of total SBA and 2.0 Msf of operational SBA in the year, and crossing 10 Msf of operational area - a first for any listed flexible workspace platform in India. City-wise, Bengaluru roughly doubled to 3.4 Msf (21% of total SBA), Pune grew to 4.3 Msf (27%), Gurugram to 2.2 Msf (14%), Mumbai to 2.0 Msf (13%), Noida to 1.4 Msf (8%) and Hyderabad to 1.3 Msf (8%). Premium mega-properties in the portfolio include Hiranandani Eastbridge, Vikhroli, Mumbai at approximately 815,000 sq. ft. and 17k seat capacity - described as the world's largest standalone flexible workspace campus - 43 EQ in Pune at approximately 613,000 sq. ft. and 15k seats, TATA Realty Intellion IT Park in Mumbai at approximately 557,000 sq. ft. and 14k seats, and Golf View Tower in Gurugram at approximately 175,000 sq. ft. and 3.5k seats. Expansion is demand-backed rather than speculative: 100% of the FY 2026-27 building requirement was locked in at year-end, over 75% of FY 2027-28 supply is already contracted and sourcing for FY 2028-29 is underway, with visibility to add 2.5-3.0 Msf of building supply annually. Bare-shell buildings are leased under campus-scale master leases of up to 15 years and passed through the centralised BuildX platform, which applies standardised fit-out modules for a predictable 45-60 day go-live; a typical centre targets breakeven and payback in 30-32 months. The mature footprint is expected to grow from 8.9 Msf at March 2026 to approximately 10.8 Msf by March 2027, and management guides an operational area of 12.5 to 13.0 Msf by March 2027. Maintenance capex runs at approximately 6-8% of Normalised gross block, equivalent to roughly 12-15% of initial capex per square foot, and maintenance capex cycles have already been completed across approximately 6 Msf of the portfolio. Of the Rs. 4,450 million gross fresh IPO proceeds, Rs. 923.61 million was earmarked for capital expenditure on fit-outs in new centres and security deposits of the new centres; as of March 31, 2026, Rs. 3,047.83 million of total fresh proceeds had been deployed and Rs. 1,402.17 million remained unutilised in the monitoring account and fixed deposits. On the sustainability side the Company is investing in a 9.9 MWp captive solar project alongside in-house lighting controls and IoT-enabled meeting rooms. Post year-end, the Board approved on June 25, 2026 the acquisition of Workstudio Spaces Pte. Ltd. through Singapore subsidiary Smartworks Space Pte. Ltd., completed on July 6, 2026, adding a step-down subsidiary.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- GCC expansion is the biggest structural demand engine; GCCs are evolving from support and shared services toward product engineering, analytics, cybersecurity, research, AI and global decision-making, requiring secure, technology-enabled, amenitised workplaces deployable quickly across cities
- Grade A office supply remains constrained - demand for Grade A office space has exceeded new completions for several consecutive years, making early access to suitable buildings strategically important and favouring operators with developer relationships, balance-sheet capacity and proven execution
- Flexible workspace has moved from tactical supplement to core corporate real-estate strategy, with enterprise-led managed office rather than small-seat coworking as the principal growth format
- The flex segment is consolidating toward larger operators with stronger balance sheets and developer relationships; the top ten operators' share of flex leasing rose from 67% in 2024 to approximately 74% by H1 2026
- Flexible workspace penetration in India stands at approximately 11-13% of Grade A stock, materially below mature global markets, leaving substantial headroom
- AI is a tailwind rather than a headwind: it compresses real-estate planning horizons and makes long-term headcount forecasting harder, increasing the value of scalable, capital-efficient workplace infrastructure over nine-year leases
- Margin lever is portfolio maturity - a rising mature-centre mix, corporate and platform costs held broadly flat over a materially larger base, and a shrinking ramp-up drag as each new investment cohort lands on a progressively larger fixed-cost base; at current scale adding capacity is no longer margin dilutive
- Competition is expected to intensify as the segment scales
- India's real GDP growth of 7.7% for FY 2025-26 and its expanding role in technology, engineering, financial services, professional services and GCCs continue to support demand for high-quality commercial infrastructure across major urban markets
- Near-term demand is expected to remain concentrated in India's major metros, with Tier II and Tier III cities a selective future expansion layer rather than a near-term driver
- Contracted rental revenue exceeded Rs. 52,000 million at year-end, covering approximately 82.5% of projected FY 2026-27 revenue - described as executed agreements with large clients, not pipeline
- 100% of the FY 2026-27 building requirement was locked in at year-end, with over 75% of FY 2027-28 supply already contracted and sourcing for FY 2028-29 underway
- SmartVantage moved from concept to an active pipeline and has secured its first large service mandates

risks.risk: Occupancy ramp-up risk on the new, immature footprint

risks.note: The model depends on a limited number of large enterprise occupiers, where a single move-out can leave material vacancy. The Company mitigates this structurally - Top 10 client revenue reduced from ~39% in FY 2018-19 to ~20% in FY 2025-26, and no single client typically occupies more than 30% of any large centre (>0.20 Msf) - but the exposure remains inherent to a large-format campus model.

Management explicitly flags cyclical fluctuations in occupancy and rental rates as characteristic of commercial real estate markets. Long-term contractual agreements with both landlords and clients are the stated buffer, but a downturn would still pressure renewals, pricing and the pace of new leasing.
risks.risk: Cyclicality of commercial real estate occupancy and rental rates

risks.risk: Dependence on access to high-quality Grade A buildings in prime micro-markets

The model depends on a limited number of large enterprise occupiers, where a single move-out can leave material vacancy. risks.risk: Data privacy, cyber-security and regulatory compliance exposure
risks.note: The Company operates technology-enabled workspaces holding sensitive data of employees, clients and partners, and states it is currently working on compliance with the DPDP rules. An Information Security Policy covering access controls, encryption, network protection and vulnerability assessment is the stated mitigation.

The INR 33 cr of security deposits paid to landlords this quarter is capital allocated to securing FY28 and FY29 supply — "We are paying today to own tomorrow's growth."

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Smartworks expanded its total super built-up area from 11.8 Msf at March 2025 to 16.1 Msf at March 2026 across 66 centres in 15 cities including Singapore, adding roughly 4.3 Msf of total SBA and 2.0 Msf of operational SBA in the year, and crossing 10 Msf of operational area - a first for any listed flexible workspace platform in India. City-wise, Bengaluru roughly doubled to 3.4 Msf (21% of total SBA), Pune grew to 4.3 Msf (27%), Gurugram to 2.2 Msf (14%), Mumbai to 2.0 Msf (13%), Noida to 1.4 Msf (8%) and Hyderabad to 1.3 Msf (8%). Premium mega-properties in the portfolio include Hiranandani Eastbridge, Vikhroli, Mumbai at approximately 815,000 sq. ft. and 17k seat capacity - described as the world's largest standalone flexible workspace campus - 43 EQ in Pune at approximately 613,000 sq. ft. and 15k seats, TATA Realty Intellion IT Park in Mumbai at approximately 557,000 sq. ft. and 14k seats, and Golf View Tower in Gurugram at approximately 175,000 sq. ft. and 3.5k seats. Expansion is demand-backed rather than speculative: 100% of the FY 2026-27 building requirement was locked in at year-end, over 75% of FY 2027-28 supply is already contracted and sourcing for FY 2028-29 is underway, with visibility to add 2.5-3.0 Msf of building supply annually. Bare-shell buildings are leased under campus-scale master leases of up to 15 years and passed through the centralised BuildX platform, which applies standardised fit-out modules for a predictable 45-60 day go-live; a typical centre targets breakeven and payback in 30-32 months. Ltd., completed on July 6, 2026, adding a step-down subsidiary.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident and unusually well-instrumented — the team quoted third-party market data (Cushman & Wakefield flex-share series), gave a specific realisation number (INR 181/sq ft vs INR 170 prior year) unprompted, and directed analysts to specific presentation slides repeatedly. moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Scale-led leasing advantage: leases whole buildings and campus areas on tenures of up to 15 years, earning preferred terms with landlords that no single-floor occupier could obtain
- Secured building supply as an operational moat: 100% of FY 2026-27 building supply locked in, with over 75% forward visibility for FY 2027-28 and FY 2028-29 sourcing underway
- Multi-year contracted revenue visibility: contracted rental revenue exceeding Rs. 52,000 million covering ~82.5% of projected FY 2026-27 revenue
- Execution speed through standardised, in-house fit-out platform BuildX enabling a predictable 45-60 day bare-shell-to-go-live transformation
- Switching cost and stickiness from large-format campuses: the 1,000+ seat cohort at ~37% of rental revenue on ~49-month tenures and ~36-month lock-ins

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Seat retention of 74% is the number that will be picked at.** Management's defence is that churn is deliberate portfolio rebalancing and mark-to-market repricing, that occupied seats rose, and that committed occupancy of mature centres remains 92% because replacement tenants are already found. Last year's full-year retention was 80–88% after a similarly weak first half.
- Occupancy dipped to 81% from 82% and is guided to 80–85% for three quarters — new-building fill, but it caps the reported metric during the heaviest growth phase.
- FCF is negative INR 56 cr and OCF/EBITDA fell below 1x. Both are explained by growth investment, but they are the first negative prints since listing.
- Concentration in H2: the guidance depends on Eastbridge and Eastside landing on schedule and pre-fills converting.
- Client-mix transition is deliberate but ongoing — IT/ITES fell from 44% to 35% over three years, and management could not break out call-centre exposure within IT/ITES when asked about AI-driven renewal risk.
- The margin-not-dilutive-at-scale claim has only been tested through one heavy capex quarter.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- The retention/occupancy pair must be read together: a 74% retention number alongside 92% committed occupancy and rising occupied seats means the company is actively repricing legacy tenants out, not losing them involuntarily. The metric will look bad in H1 and recover by year-end, as it did last year.
- VAS is structurally more attractive than it looks because it is take-rate, not resale — no cost sits on the books, so it hits the bottom line directly. It tripled YoY and is explicitly excluded from guidance.
- The GCC revenue already booked understates the opportunity: the services layer for signed GCCs has not started billing because most offices are still under fit-out — "the value accretion of the other services over and above the space will happen… over the next two or three quarters."

- Landlord mix is ~65% non-institutional / 35% institutional and is expected to stay roughly there — the institutional share is the completion hedge, not the whole strategy.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Grow only where demand is already visible - expansion is executed against revenue and buildings already signed rather than against forecast demand, so tomorrow's campuses are contracted today
- Concentrate on large-format, campus-scale managed offices for mid-to-large enterprises rather than small-seat coworking, deliberately moving away from traditional volatile coworking layouts
